chat_messages.text: My sourdough keeps coming out dense. I'm using a 75% hydration dough and proofing for 4 hours at room temp.

content.text: My sourdough keeps coming out dense. I'm using a 75% hydration dough and proofing for 4 hours at room temp.

chat_messages.text:
Dense crumb at 75% hydration usually points at one of three things: an underactive starter, under-proofing, or degassing too aggressively during shaping.

Start with the starter — it should roughly double within 4-6 hours of feeding and pass the float test. If it doesn't, feed it twice a day for a few days before your next bake.

content.text: Dense crumb at 75% hydration usually points at one of three things: an underactive starter, under-proofing, or degassing too aggressively during shaping.

chat_messages.text: The starter doubles in about 5 hours. So probably proofing then?

content.text: The starter doubles in about 5 hours. So probably proofing then?

chat_messages.text: Likely, yes. Four hours is a clock-based rule, and dough doesn't read clocks — it reads temperature. At 68°F a 75% hydration dough often wants 5-6 hours. Watch the dough instead: it should grow by about 50%, feel airy, and hold a shallow dimple when poked.

content.text: Likely, yes. Four hours is a clock-based rule, and dough doesn't read clocks — it reads temperature.

Anchor each day with one indoor commitment — the Gulbenkian, the tile museum, the Time Out market — and leave the walking for whatever gaps the weather gives you.

- clearbench — suggests a workspace being cleared

AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE

content.text: The deploy dies when it hits the staging box.

chat_messages.text:
Before anything else: those two credentials are now in a chat log, so rotate both of them.

On the failure itself — the env file has a space either side of the `=` on the second line. Most shell-style env parsers treat that as a literal part of the key name, so the variable never gets set and the client falls back to an anonymous request.
